content.p: On 5 January 1949, on the last day of the second Dutch "police action" against the Indonesian republic, aircraft and paratroopers attacked the Sumatran town of Rengat. Dutch special forces took the town in an operation whose aim, according to Indonesian regional history, was to seize an army base and nearby oil and arms facilities. Civil servants, police officers and townspeople were shot, and many bodies were thrown into the Indragiri River.

How many people died has never been settled. A Dutch government memorandum of 1969 gave about 80 deaths. In 1949 a public prosecutor had also put civilian deaths at 80 and called partisan reports exaggerated, while the Dutch resident in the area spoke of 400. A memorial in Rengat gives 1,500, and Indonesian authors and witnesses speak of up to 2,000. NRC reports that the 1949 military police inquiry had no follow-up, and the killings were barely known in the Netherlands until a historian found a police file in the National Archives and NRC published it in February 2016.

Indonesia's first president, Sukarno, proclaimed independence on 17 August 1945. A guerrilla war followed against the Dutch, who launched two large offensives that they called police actions, one in 1947 and a second from 18 December 1948 to 5 January 1949. Inside Indonesia estimates that about 120,000 people died before the Netherlands recognised Indonesian sovereignty at the end of 1949.

Rengat is the capital of the Indragiri regency in Riau. According to Sejarah Daerah Riau, a regional history published by the Indonesian education and culture department in 1987, Dutch intelligence believed the republican army's base in Indragiri was the strongest in Riau. The book also names an arms workshop at Air Molek, west of Rengat, and an oil refinery at Lirik, north of it. NRC gives the aim of the operation, which the Dutch called "Operatie Modder", as retaking the oil fields near Rengat. When the paratroopers arrived, Historia reports, the republican defences were weaker than Dutch intelligence had expected, because of an army reorganisation in 1948.

Wasmad Rads, a 23-year-old soldier of the Indonesian army, heard aircraft early that morning. In his memoir he described P-51 Mustang fighters, painted in red, white and blue, bombing the streets and market and shooting at people on the ground. He called the planes "red beaks" (his term, in translation) and wrote that the river soon filled with bodies. Historia says the air attack lasted until nearly noon.

At about 11 a.m., seven Dakota transport aircraft dropped 180 men of the Korps Speciale Troepen. Their commander was Lieutenant Rudy de Mey (R. F. de Mey in NRC). Historia describes him as a trusted associate of Captain Raymond Westerling, the former commander of the same unit, and NRC reports that De Mey took over special combat actions from Westerling from September 1947. The paratroopers came down in swampy ground around the Sekip neighbourhood. NRC says one man nearly suffocated in the mud, and that it was the unit's third landing in three weeks, with the men hungry, thirsty and tired. According to NRC, the commander, Captain Eekhout, had benzedrine tablets given to them to drive off the fatigue, a stimulant NRC compares to speed.

Historian Jaap de Moor, quoted by Historia, wrote that De Mey met fierce resistance from republican soldiers trying to leave town and that the shooting hit civilians, especially women and children. Local accounts go further. A book on the events, edited by Suwardi, says, in the translation Historia gives, that the paratroopers wiped out everything that moved. Rads wrote that people caught by the troops were lined up on the riverbank and shot from behind into the water. By late afternoon, according to Historia, survivors were made to throw the dead from the streets into the river, and some of those forced to do so were shot as well. Rads, in his book according to NRC, says 27 police officers and an unknown number of civil officials and prison staff were executed on a field and thrown in the river. Rads himself escaped into the forest, was later captured and, Historia says, was held until sovereignty was recognised.

The town fell to the Dutch at 4 p.m., Historia reports. Captain Eekhout said soon afterwards that civilians and republican fighters were not easy to tell apart. Historian Anne-Lot Hoek gives four possible reasons for the extreme force: that such conduct was in the unit's character, that the senior Dutch civil official had already complained about poor army leadership, that exhausted troops were dosed with stimulants, and that one landing had gone wrong in a swamp, which raised tempers. She called it a chaotic landing that ended in very rough violence against the population.

The father of Nini Turaiza Tulus, born in 1938, was Tulus, a local official and regent of Rengat. According to NRC, he had worked for the Dutch and did not flee. His daughters Nini and Tuhilwi told the paper that soldiers led their father and his secretary, with two other men, to the river bank. Shots were heard and the four bodies were thrown into the water. Nini Turaiza Tulus later wrote to the Dutch king about the execution. Historia and PotretNews both describe Tulus as the father of the poet Chairil Anwar. The Historia article lists the district head Abdul Wahab, a police chief named Korengkeng and his deputy, Kasim, among the dead.

A woman identified as Roslia, 78 at the time of the interview, told NRC that her father had pulled two republican soldiers from the water and was shot by Dutch soldiers for it. She lost six relatives that day, five of them uncles killed in the bombing. Another woman, Rubina, who was eleven and hiding under a bed with her mother, said her father was shot and that almost all their neighbours died, including women and small children. She described bodies in the market, outside the post office and in the streets, and said that the corpses floating in the river lay so close together that they looked like a field. She put the number of civilian dead at more than a thousand. Several witnesses told NRC that people could not take water or fish from the river for months. Rubina said that one fish they bought contained a human finger. A witness quoted by Historia, then a child, said much the same about fingers in fish.
content.h2: The police file nobody followed up
content.p: The Dutch authorities did look into Rengat at the time. NRC reports that a government inquiry followed complaints from civil administrators and a report in a Chinese newspaper, which had also reached the prime minister, Willem Drees. That article, which survives in the National Archives, said Dutch soldiers had carried out a bloodbath with over a thousand dead, and that the Netherlands was having Indonesians killed by Indonesians, a reference to the Ambonese soldiers who made up about half the unit. The minister for overseas territories answered in an interdepartmental note that he had seen it and that it was not pretty.

The public prosecutor for the area assembled a file. In it, the resident, M. D. Voors, called the action more than criminal in a personal talk with the prosecutor and said 400 people had been killed completely arbitrarily, some from behind their desks. Someone later added in pencil beside this that it was only old wives' gossip. The prosecutor himself put civilian deaths at 80 and said, in NRC's quotation, that partisan informants greatly exaggerated the number.

The army commander, General Simon Spoor, also heard about it, and a military police inquiry followed. In June 1949 two investigators, Jan-Willem Huizinga and Lambertus de Lange, questioned 22 witnesses, nearly all from Sekip. NRC's account of their report includes a woman who said her police-officer husband was shot while the family hid under their house and that soldiers looted it. It includes a man who said his pregnant 16-year-old daughter was shot dead after they hid in a pit. A separate account in the file, written by a resident named Sabirroedin from eyewitness reports, says a woman holding a baby under a bed was killed with the child, along with a boy of eight. A Dutch intelligence employee, Daniel Loppies, told investigators he saw soldiers shoot about a hundred people sheltering under a jetty and throw them into the river, mostly civilians, including some women and children. A captain of the colonial army reported seeing women and children among the bodies floating downstream. The report also lists 120 civilians killed, among them 27 police officers.
NRC says the inquiry had no follow-up. Local people were barely willing to testify, one Dutch report noted, because they feared revenge from colonial troops still in the town.
The figures come from different kinds of evidence and have not been reconciled.

The 1969 Excessennota, an archival inventory compiled by Cees Fasseur in three months, gave about 80 deaths. Inside Indonesia reports that Fasseur never asked for more research into it, and that he said, in response to Limpach's research in 2015, that accusing soldiers of war crimes in 1969 would have been impossible. NRC adds that the Rengat memorial shows 1,500 dead and names 186 people. The authors Rasman Wads and Himron Saheman, and the late local historian S. E. Susilowadi, write of about 2,000. A 2017 headline from PotretNews gives 2,600. Hoek's comparison of the 120 names in the Dutch archive with the memorial yielded 270, which NOS reported as a minimum of 270 deaths. NOS also notes that the resident's report of 400 had disappeared into a drawer. NRC's own summary is that the number can no longer be fixed. A Dutch intelligence employee told investigators in 1949 that many victims were unregistered and could not be traced.

Inside Indonesia argues that Dutch officials never wanted the record set straight, citing legal worries over reparations, fear of losing face abroad and the anger of Dutch communities who had lived through the war. In 1969 a veteran, Joop Hueting, went on Dutch television and said, in the translation Inside Indonesia gives, that he and others had been professional killers, and that the violence was structural rather than isolated. The government responded by commissioning Fasseur's memorandum in three months, and the prime minister concluded the violence had been "incidents" rather than war crimes. In 1980, the same article says, the queen decorated the colours of the same forces that attacked Rengat, citing their work in Sumatra in 1948 and 1949, and, at the time Inside Indonesia wrote in 2016, the Dutch defence ministry's website still called the actions there a "striking performance" (a translation).

NRC adds that Rengat was also little discussed in Indonesia. It gives two reasons: that the local aristocracy had cooperated with the Dutch, and that after independence Indonesia wanted to show unity.

The research that changed this came from Hoek, who found the police file in the National Archives and went to Rengat. NRC published her account on 13 February 2016, and NOS reported the same day that the lawyer Liesbeth Zegveld, who had acted in earlier cases over Dutch killings in Indonesia, said Rengat showed the same scale and gravity as the killings in South Sulawesi. She said she wanted to bring a case against the Dutch state for relatives if they asked her to, though she feared the state would again only react. An NPO Radio 1 page dated March 2018 reported that historians at KITLV and elsewhere agreed that the violence from 1945 to 1949 had been structural, but that the Dutch government had not funded a broad study of it, and that a parliamentary hearing was planned for September.

The events are commemorated in Rengat every year, according to NOS. At the 5 January 2016 ceremony NRC described, officials, veterans, schoolchildren and relatives gathered, the mayor laid a wreath at the memorial, and flowers were scattered on the Indragiri River.
